description: A clear, accurate lesson on block headers and Merkle trees (Mastering Bitcoin ch. 11).

messages.text: Today: what's inside a block. A block is a container: a small header plus the list of transactions.
The header is only 80 bytes. The transactions are much bigger, often hundreds of kilobytes or more.
The header has a few fields: the version, the hash of the previous block's header, the Merkle root, a timestamp, the difficulty target and a nonce.
The previous block hash is what links blocks into a chain. Each header points back to its parent.
A block is identified by hashing its header twice with SHA256. That block hash isn't stored in the block itself.
Now the Merkle root. It's a single hash that summarises every transaction in the block.
Picture a tournament bracket. Each transaction is hashed. Then neighbouring hashes are paired, joined together and hashed again.
You keep pairing and hashing level by level until one hash is left. That's the Merkle root.
Bitcoin uses double SHA256 here too: SHA256 applied twice.
If a level has an odd number of hashes, the last one is duplicated so it has a partner.
The root goes in the header. Change any transaction and its hash changes, which changes every hash above it, so the root changes.
That's why the header commits to the whole set of transactions, even though it's tiny.
Why bother? Lightweight clients, like phone wallets, don't download every transaction. They mostly keep headers.
To prove a transaction is in a block, a full node sends a Merkle path: the sibling hashes along the way from that transaction up to the root.
The path is about log2 of N hashes, where N is the number of transactions. For a few thousand transactions that's around a dozen hashes.
The client rehashes up the path and checks the result matches the Merkle root in the header it already has. If it matches, the transaction is in the block.
